items.summary: The Network tab is where most frontend bugs are actually solved. A blank screen, a spinner that never ends, a form that "does nothing": open the Network tab and the answer is usually one row away. Most developers use about a fifth of it. This guide goes through the rest: the filters, the details panes, the right-click menu, and the features hidden under More tools . Everything here is Chrome's DevTools, and the same in Edge and other Chromium browsers. Firefox's Network Monitor has most of the same features under slightly different names. Opening it, and the first trap ​ Open DevTools with F12 , Ctrl+Shift+I (Windows, Linux) or Cmd+Option+I (macOS), then pick Network . You can also right-click anything on the page, choose Inspect , and switch tabs. The first trap: the Network tab only records while DevTools is open. Requests made before you opened it are not there. Reload the page ( Ctrl+R / Cmd+R ) with DevTools open to capture everything from the first byte. The toolbar ​ From left to right, the controls you will use most: Record ( Ctrl+E / Cmd+E ): stop recording to freeze the list while you inspect it. Clear ( Ctrl+L / Cmd+K on macOS): empty the list before reproducing a bug, so only the relevant requests are left. Preserve log : keep requests across navigations. Without it, a redirect or a form submit that reloads the page wipes the request you wanted to see. Turn it on for login flows and anything that navigates. Disable cache : skip the HTTP cache while DevTools is open. Use it when you are asking "did my change deploy?" and want every file fetched fresh. Throttling : the dropdown that says No throttling . Presets such as Fast 4G, Slow 4G and 3G slow every request down, and Offline cuts the tab off. You can add your own profile with custom download, upload and latency. Import / Export HAR : the up and down arrows. More on HAR files below. The gear icon on the right holds four display settings worth knowing: Big request rows (two lines per row: transferred and real size, time and latency), Show overview (the timeline strip at the top), Group by frame , and Capture screenshots (filmstrip of the page as it loads). Filtering: find the one request ​ A busy page makes hundreds of requests. The filter row is how you find yours. Type buttons. All , Fetch/XHR , Doc , CSS , JS , Font , Img , Media , Manifest , Socket , Wasm , Other . For API debugging, Fetch/XHR is the one. Ctrl+click (or Cmd+click ) selects several. Text filter. Type part of the url. Wrap it in slashes for a regular expression ( /api\/v[12]\// ), prefix it with - to hide what matches ( -analytics ), or tick Invert . Property filters. The filter box understands property:value , and this is the part most people never discover. Start typing and DevTools suggests them: Filter Shows status-code:500 Responses with that status method:POST Requests with that method domain:api.example.com Requests to that host ( *.example.com works) -domain:*.google-analytics.com Everything except that host mime-type:application/json Responses of that type larger-than:100k Responses bigger than 100 KB has-response-header:Set-Cookie Responses carrying that header is:running Requests still in flight scheme:http Requests not on https Combine them with spaces: method:POST status-code:422 domain:api.example.com is every failed form submit to your API. Search. Ctrl+F / Cmd+F with the Network tab focused opens a search across urls, headers and response bodies . When you know a value is on screen but not which request delivered it, search for the value. Reading the request list ​ The default columns are Name , Status , Type , Initiator , Size , Time and Waterfall . Right-click any column header to add more: Method , Domain , Protocol (spot an HTTP/1.1 request among HTTP/2 ones), Priority , Remote address , or any response header you name under Response Headers > Manage header columns . A few values worth recognising: Status in red, (failed) , (canceled) , (blocked:...) : the request never got a normal answer. Hover it, or open it, for the net::ERR_... reason. CORS error in the Status column : the server answered, but the browser refused to hand the response to the page. See How to fix CORS errors in your browser . Size (memory cache) or (disk cache) : nothing came over the network. If you expected a fresh response, this is why you are not seeing your change. Size (ServiceWorker) : a service worker answered the request. If your app uses one (or Mock Service Worker ), this is where its responses show up. A row with method OPTIONS right before your request : a CORS preflight. Initiator tells you who made the request: a script with a line number, a stylesheet, the parser. Hover it for the full JavaScript call stack, and click a frame to jump to the code. Hold Shift while hovering a row to colour its initiators green and the requests it caused red. Inspecting one request ​ Click a row to open its details. The tabs: Headers. The url, method, status and remote address at the top, then Response Headers and Request Headers . Toggle Raw to see them exactly as sent. A yellow "Provisional headers are shown" warning means DevTools did not see the final request (served from cache, or blocked before it left); the headers listed are what the browser intended to send. Payload. What you sent: query string parameters, the JSON body, form fields. View source shows the raw body, View parsed a tree. If the server says your request is wrong, check here before you check the server. Preview. The response, formatted: a collapsible tree for JSON, a rendered image, a rendered HTML page. Response. The raw response body. On a large minified JSON, the {} button at the bottom pretty-prints it. Initiator. The same call stack as the column, plus the chain of requests that led to this one. Timing. Where the time went, phase by phase: Phase A long one usually means Queueing / Stalled Too many requests to one host at once, or a lower priority DNS Lookup A new domain; consider dns-prefetch or preconnect Initial connection, SSL A new connection; reuse connections, preconnect Request sent A large upload Waiting for server response The server is slow to start answering (time to first byte) Content Download A large response, or a slow connection Cookies. The cookies sent and set by this request, and the reason any was blocked ( SameSite , Secure , third-party restrictions). Messages (WebSockets) and EventStream (server-sent events) appear for those requests and list each message as it arrives. The right-click menu ​ Right-click a request for the actions that make the Network tab a tool rather than a log: Copy > Copy as cURL : the exact request, headers and cookies included, as a terminal command. Paste it in a bug report and the backend developer can reproduce it without your browser. Copy as fetch and Copy as Node.js fetch do the same in JavaScript. Copy > Copy response : the body, ready to paste into a fixture or a mock. Replay XHR (on Fetch/XHR requests): send it again, as is. Handy after a backend fix. Block request URL / Block request domain : the request fails from now on, with a network error. Quick check of "what breaks when this script does not load?" Override content / Override headers : see local overrides below. Save all as HAR : export the whole list. Copying a request with credentials (cURL, fetch, HAR) copies your cookies and tokens too. Treat the result like a password. Features under More tools ​ Open them from the DevTools menu (the three dots) > More tools , or with the command menu ( Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P ) and their name. Network request blocking. A list of url patterns ( */api/recommendations* ) that all fail while the panel is enabled. Easier to manage than the right-click action when you block several things. Network conditions. Change the user agent (test what your server does for a mobile browser or a bot), turn off the cache, pick a throttling profile, and set the Accept-Language the browser sends. Local overrides: change a response ​ Local overrides let you replace a response with a file on your disk, and the replacement survives reloads. Right-click a request and pick Override content . The first time, DevTools asks for a folder to keep overrides in, and permission to use it. Edit the response in the Sources panel and save. The request now shows a purple dot in the Network tab, and the page receives your version. Override headers does the same for response headers. Overrides are good for one quick experiment on a single file: a changed script, a stylesheet, a JSON response. HAR files: share a whole session ​ A HAR file is the Network tab saved to disk: every request, header, timing and (optionally) body. Export one with the down-arrow icon, and someone else can import it with the up-arrow and inspect your session as if they had been there. It is the best attachment for a "it fails for me" bug report. Recent versions of Chrome leave sensitive data such as cookies out of the export by default; still read a HAR before you share it. We wrote a whole post on what a HAR file tells a developer . Where the Network tab stops ​ The Network tab is excellent at observing traffic. It is limited at changing it: Blocking only produces network errors. You cannot make an endpoint return a 500 , a 401 or a 429 to see your error screens. Overrides cannot change the status code , take a few steps per request, need a local folder, and only apply while DevTools is open. It cannot change a request before it is sent: its url, its body, a header the page sets. Nothing is shared. Your overrides and blocked patterns live in your DevTools, not in a file the team can reuse. This is the gap a browser extension like tweak fills, and it works next to DevTools rather than instead of it: Mock rules return any status, body, headers and delay for a url, without DevTools open. See How to test error states in your frontend application . Modify rules take the real response and change one field, the status or a header (Tweak Basic and Tweak Max). Headers only rules , redirect rules and block rules are applied by the browser itself, on every request type, page navigations included. Pause & Edit holds a request before it is sent so you can edit it (Tweak Max). Request capture records what the tab sends and turns any request into a rule in one pick, and a HAR file exported from the Network tab imports as rules on every plan. Cheat sheet ​ Task How See requests from page load Open DevTools, then reload Keep requests across a redirect Preserve log Only API calls Fetch/XHR type button Only failures status-code:500 (or -status-code:200 ) Hide analytics noise -domain:*.google-analytics.com Find which request returned a value Ctrl+F / Cmd+F , search response bodies Why is it slow? Timing tab Who made this request? Initiator column, hover for the stack Reproduce it in a terminal Right-click > Copy as cURL What breaks without it? Right-click > Block request URL Test on a slow network Throttling dropdown Share the session Export HAR Return a 500 / change a response for good A tweak Mock rule If you liked this article, consider sharing ( tweeting ) it to your followers. Did you like this article? Yes No Need something else? Request a feature Thanks for your feedback!

  • Clear (Ctrl+L / Cmd+K on macOS): empty the list before reproducing a bug, so only the relevant requests are left.
  • Preserve log: keep requests across navigations. Without it, a redirect or a form submit that reloads the page wipes the request you wanted to see. Turn it on for login flows and anything that navigates.
  • Disable cache: skip the HTTP cache while DevTools is open. Use it when you are asking "did my change deploy?" and want every file fetched fresh.
  • Throttling: the dropdown that says No throttling. Presets such as Fast 4G, Slow 4G and 3G slow every request down, and Offline cuts the tab off. You can add your own profile with custom download, upload and latency.
  • Import / Export HAR: the up and down arrows. More on HAR files below.

The gear icon on the right holds four display settings worth knowing: Big request rows (two lines per row: transferred and real size, time and latency), Show overview (the timeline strip at the top), Group by frame, and Capture screenshots (filmstrip of the page as it loads).

Filtering: find the one request​

A busy page makes hundreds of requests. The filter row is how you find yours.

Type buttons. All, Fetch/XHR, Doc, CSS, JS, Font, Img, Media, Manifest, Socket, Wasm, Other. For API debugging, Fetch/XHR is the one. Ctrl+click (or Cmd+click) selects several.

Text filter. Type part of the url. Wrap it in slashes for a regular expression (/api\/v[12]\//), prefix it with - to hide what matches (-analytics), or tick Invert.

Property filters. The filter box understands property:value, and this is the part most people never discover. Start typing and DevTools suggests them:

FilterShowsstatus-code:500Responses with that statusmethod:POSTRequests with that methoddomain:api.example.comRequests to that host (*.example.com works)-domain:*.google-analytics.comEverything except that hostmime-type:application/jsonResponses of that typelarger-than:100kResponses bigger than 100 KBhas-response-header:Set-CookieResponses carrying that headeris:runningRequests still in flightscheme:httpRequests not on https

Combine them with spaces: method:POST status-code:422 domain:api.example.com is every failed form submit to your API.

Search. Ctrl+F / Cmd+F with the Network tab focused opens a search across urls, headers and response bodies. When you know a value is on screen but not which request delivered it, search for the value.

Reading the request list​

The default columns are Name, Status, Type, Initiator, Size, Time and Waterfall. Right-click any column header to add more: Method, Domain, Protocol (spot an HTTP/1.1 request among HTTP/2 ones), Priority, Remote address, or any response header you name under Response Headers > Manage header columns.

A few values worth recognising:

  • Status in red, (failed), (canceled), (blocked:...): the request never got a normal answer. Hover it, or open it, for the net::ERR_... reason.
  • CORS error in the Status column: the server answered, but the browser refused to hand the response to the page. See How to fix CORS errors in your browser.
  • Size (memory cache) or (disk cache): nothing came over the network. If you expected a fresh response, this is why you are not seeing your change.
  • Size (ServiceWorker): a service worker answered the request. If your app uses one (or Mock Service Worker), this is where its responses show up.
  • A row with method OPTIONS right before your request: a CORS preflight.

Initiator tells you who made the request: a script with a line number, a stylesheet, the parser. Hover it for the full JavaScript call stack, and click a frame to jump to the code. Hold Shift while hovering a row to colour its initiators green and the requests it caused red.

Inspecting one request​

Click a row to open its details. The tabs:

Headers. The url, method, status and remote address at the top, then Response Headers and Request Headers. Toggle Raw to see them exactly as sent. A yellow "Provisional headers are shown" warning means DevTools did not see the final request (served from cache, or blocked before it left); the headers listed are what the browser intended to send.

Payload. What you sent: query string parameters, the JSON body, form fields. View source shows the raw body, View parsed a tree. If the server says your request is wrong, check here before you check the server.

Preview. The response, formatted: a collapsible tree for JSON, a rendered image, a rendered HTML page.

Response. The raw response body. On a large minified JSON, the {} button at the bottom pretty-prints it.

Initiator. The same call stack as the column, plus the chain of requests that led to this one.

Timing. Where the time went, phase by phase:

PhaseA long one usually meansQueueing / StalledToo many requests to one host at once, or a lower priorityDNS LookupA new domain; consider dns-prefetch or preconnectInitial connection, SSLA new connection; reuse connections, preconnectRequest sentA large uploadWaiting for server responseThe server is slow to start answering (time to first byte)Content DownloadA large response, or a slow connection

Cookies. The cookies sent and set by this request, and the reason any was blocked (SameSite, Secure, third-party restrictions).

Messages (WebSockets) and EventStream (server-sent events) appear for those requests and list each message as it arrives.

The right-click menu​

Right-click a request for the actions that make the Network tab a tool rather than a log:

  • Copy > Copy as cURL: the exact request, headers and cookies included, as a terminal command. Paste it in a bug report and the backend developer can reproduce it without your browser. Copy as fetch and Copy as Node.js fetch do the same in JavaScript.
  • Copy > Copy response: the body, ready to paste into a fixture or a mock.
  • Replay XHR (on Fetch/XHR requests): send it again, as is. Handy after a backend fix.
  • Block request URL / Block request domain: the request fails from now on, with a network error. Quick check of "what breaks when this script does not load?"
  • Override content / Override headers: see local overrides below.
  • Save all as HAR: export the whole list.

Copying a request with credentials (cURL, fetch, HAR) copies your cookies and tokens too. Treat the result like a password.

Features under More tools​

Open them from the DevTools menu (the three dots) > More tools, or with the command menu (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P) and their name.

Network request blocking. A list of url patterns (*/api/recommendations*) that all fail while the panel is enabled. Easier to manage than the right-click action when you block several things.

Network conditions. Change the user agent (test what your server does for a mobile browser or a bot), turn off the cache, pick a throttling profile, and set the Accept-Language the browser sends.

Local overrides: change a response​

Local overrides let you replace a response with a file on your disk, and the replacement survives reloads.

  1. Right-click a request and pick Override content.
  2. The first time, DevTools asks for a folder to keep overrides in, and permission to use it.
  3. Edit the response in the Sources panel and save. The request now shows a purple dot in the Network tab, and the page receives your version.

Override headers does the same for response headers. Overrides are good for one quick experiment on a single file: a changed script, a stylesheet, a JSON response.

HAR files: share a whole session​

A HAR file is the Network tab saved to disk: every request, header, timing and (optionally) body. Export one with the down-arrow icon, and someone else can import it with the up-arrow and inspect your session as if they had been there. It is the best attachment for a "it fails for me" bug report. Recent versions of Chrome leave sensitive data such as cookies out of the export by default; still read a HAR before you share it. We wrote a whole post on what a HAR file tells a developer.

Where the Network tab stops​

The Network tab is excellent at observing traffic. It is limited at changing it:

  • Blocking only produces network errors. You cannot make an endpoint return a 500, a 401 or a 429 to see your error screens.
  • Overrides cannot change the status code, take a few steps per request, need a local folder, and only apply while DevTools is open.
  • It cannot change a request before it is sent: its url, its body, a header the page sets.
  • Nothing is shared. Your overrides and blocked patterns live in your DevTools, not in a file the team can reuse.

This is the gap a browser extension like tweak fills, and it works next to DevTools rather than instead of it:

  • Mock rules return any status, body, headers and delay for a url, without DevTools open. See How to test error states in your frontend application.
  • Modify rules take the real response and change one field, the status or a header (Tweak Basic and Tweak Max).
  • Headers only rules, redirect rules and block rules are applied by the browser itself, on every request type, page navigations included.
  • Pause & Edit holds a request before it is sent so you can edit it (Tweak Max).
  • Request capture records what the tab sends and turns any request into a rule in one pick, and a HAR file exported from the Network tab imports as rules on every plan.
Cheat sheet​ TaskHowSee requests from page loadOpen DevTools, then reloadKeep requests across a redirectPreserve logOnly API callsFetch/XHR type buttonOnly failuresstatus-code:500 (or -status-code:200)Hide analytics noise-domain:*.google-analytics.comFind which request returned a valueCtrl+F / Cmd+F, search response bodiesWhy is it slow?Timing tabWho made this request?Initiator column, hover for the stackReproduce it in a terminalRight-click > Copy as cURLWhat breaks without it?Right-click > Block request URLTest on a slow networkThrottling dropdownShare the sessionExport HARReturn a 500 / change a response for goodA tweak Mock rule

items.summary: You call an API from your frontend, the request shows up in the Network tab with a perfectly good response, and your code still gets nothing but this in the console: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/orders' from origin 'http://localhost:5173' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. An origin is the scheme, host and port together, so localhost:5173 and localhost:3000 are different origins too. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how the server says it is fine: with Access-Control-* response headers. No header, no access. The request usually did reach the server, which is why you see a response in DevTools, but the browser refuses to hand it to your JavaScript. Two consequences matter for debugging: CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server. The same request works from curl or Postman, because they are not browsers. "It works in Postman" tells you nothing about CORS. The fix is a header on the response. Nothing you change in your frontend fetch call will make a missing header appear. The server must answer it with a successful status and the right headers, or the real request is never sent. In the Network tab, you will see the preflight as a separate row with the method OPTIONS . The common ones: Message contains What is wrong No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present The response has no CORS headers at all Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check The OPTIONS request failed: missing headers, or a non-2xx status (often 404 or 405 ) Method PUT is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods The preflight answer does not list your method Request header field authorization is not allowed The preflight answer does not list a header you send must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include' You send cookies ( credentials: 'include' ), so the server must name your origin, not * The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header contains multiple values Two layers (app and proxy) both add the header Firefox words them differently ("Cross-Origin Request Blocked … Reason: CORS header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' missing"), but the reasons map one to one. Asking for a CORS change takes days. You need to keep working now. What not to do ​ mode: 'no-cors' does not fix anything. It makes the request succeed with an opaque response: your code cannot read the body or the status. It only silences the error. Launching the browser with web security disabled ( --disable-web-security ) turns off the same-origin policy for every site in that profile, including your bank. If you do it, use a throwaway profile and never browse with it. Public CORS proxies send your requests, and whatever tokens they carry, through someone else's server. The template matches every url ( .* ). Change it to your API's host, for example api\.example\.com , so only those responses are touched. Keep the scope on Active tab. That is the default: the headers only apply on the tab where tweak is running, and stop when you stop tweak. Global applies them everywhere, all the time, which is easy to forget. Add Authorization if you send it. By the CORS standard, Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * does not cover the Authorization header. If your preflight still fails on it, change that row's value to *, Authorization . What the template deliberately does not do ​ Cookies and credentials. items.summary_html:
You call an API from your frontend, the request shows up in the Network tab with a perfectly good response, and your code still gets nothing but this in the console:

Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/orders' from origin 'http://localhost:5173'
has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on
the requested resource.

This post explains what the browser is doing, how to read the variations of that message, how to fix it properly, and how to get unblocked right now while you develop, with one click.

What CORS is, in one minute​

Browsers apply the same-origin policy: a page on http://localhost:5173 may send a request to https://api.example.com, but it may not read the response unless that server says it is fine. An origin is the scheme, host and port together, so localhost:5173 and localhost:3000 are different origins too.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how the server says it is fine: with Access-Control-* response headers. No header, no access. The request usually did reach the server, which is why you see a response in DevTools, but the browser refuses to hand it to your JavaScript.

Two consequences matter for debugging:

  • CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server. The same request works from curl or Postman, because they are not browsers. "It works in Postman" tells you nothing about CORS.
  • The fix is a header on the response. Nothing you change in your frontend fetch call will make a missing header appear.
Preflight requests​

For anything beyond a simple GET or form POST (a PUT, a DELETE, a JSON body, an Authorization header, a custom header), the browser first sends an OPTIONS request, the preflight, asking for permission. The server must answer it with a successful status and the right headers, or the real request is never sent. In the Network tab, you will see the preflight as a separate row with the method OPTIONS.

Reading the error message​

The console message tells you exactly which check failed. The common ones:

Message containsWhat is wrongNo 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is presentThe response has no CORS headers at allResponse to preflight request doesn't pass access control checkThe OPTIONS request failed: missing headers, or a non-2xx status (often 404 or 405)Method PUT is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-MethodsThe preflight answer does not list your methodRequest header field authorization is not allowedThe preflight answer does not list a header you sendmust not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'You send cookies (credentials: 'include'), so the server must name your origin, not *The 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header contains multiple valuesTwo layers (app and proxy) both add the header

Firefox words them differently ("Cross-Origin Request Blocked … Reason: CORS header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' missing"), but the reasons map one to one.

The right fix: the server​

In production, CORS is fixed where it is enforced from: the server's response. Configure your API (or the gateway in front of it) to answer with:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

Every framework has a middleware for it (cors for Express, django-cors-headers, rack-cors, Spring's @CrossOrigin...). Two rules: name the origins you trust instead of reflecting whatever the request sends, and make sure OPTIONS requests reach the middleware rather than a 404 route.

In local development: a proxy​

If the API is yours and you only hit CORS on localhost, the cleanest fix is often to stop being cross-origin. Every dev server can proxy API calls through its own origin:

// vite.config.js
export default {
  server: {
    proxy: {
      '/api': { target: 'https://api.example.com', changeOrigin: true },
    },
  },
}

Your code calls /api/orders, the dev server forwards it, and the browser sees a same-origin request. webpack's devServer.proxy and Next.js rewrites do the same.

When you cannot change the server​

Often the API is not yours: a third-party service, a staging backend owned by another team, a production API you are debugging against from localhost. Asking for a CORS change takes days. You need to keep working now.

What not to do​
  • mode: 'no-cors' does not fix anything. It makes the request succeed with an opaque response: your code cannot read the body or the status. It only silences the error.
  • Launching the browser with web security disabled (--disable-web-security) turns off the same-origin policy for every site in that profile, including your bank. If you do it, use a throwaway profile and never browse with it.
  • Public CORS proxies send your requests, and whatever tokens they carry, through someone else's server.
Unblock CORS with tweak's CORS unblock template​

tweak can add the CORS headers to responses in your browser, on the requests you choose, without touching the server and without disabling anything globally. You do not have to know which headers: there is a ready-made template for it.

  1. Install tweak and open it on the tab where the error happens.
  2. Add a rule, open its rule type list, and click See more options and templates under it.
  3. Search cors and pick CORS unblock.
  4. Start tweak on the tab and reload the page.

The template turns the rule into a headers only rule that sets four response headers:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *
Access-Control-Expose-Headers: *

These are applied by the browser itself, so they reach every request on the tab, not only fetch and XMLHttpRequest. The rule is free, on every plan, and it arrives with notes explaining what it does.

After that it is an ordinary rule you can edit. Three edits worth making:

  • Narrow the url. The template matches every url (.*). Change it to your API's host, for example api\.example\.com, so only those responses are touched.
  • Keep the scope on Active tab. That is the default: the headers only apply on the tab where tweak is running, and stop when you stop tweak. Global applies them everywhere, all the time, which is easy to forget.
  • Add Authorization if you send it. By the CORS standard, Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * does not cover the Authorization header. If your preflight still fails on it, change that row's value to *, Authorization.
What the template deliberately does not do​
  • Cookies and credentials. A request with credentials: 'include' is refused when the response says Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, and the browser requires Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true on top. The template ships without that row on purpose: * is the only origin it can set for every site, and the combination would look like it works while the browser still refuses it. For a credentialed API, edit the rule: set Access-Control-Allow-Origin to your page's exact origin (http://localhost:5173) and add an Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true row.
  • A preflight the server rejects. If the server answers OPTIONS with a 404 or 405, adding headers does not change the status, and the browser still refuses. Fix the server, or use the next option.
Or skip the network entirely: mock the response​

If what you need is the data, not the real server, a Mock rule answers the request inside the page with the payload you give it. The request never leaves the browser, so there is no cross-origin response and no CORS check at all. Use request capture to record the real response once and prefill the mock from it.

Checklist​
  1. Read the console message: which check failed?
  2. Open the Network tab: is there an OPTIONS preflight, and what did it return?
  3. Your server? Fix the headers there, or proxy through your dev server.
  4. Not your server? Use tweak's CORS unblock template, narrowed to the API's url, on the active tab.
  5. Sending cookies? Name the exact origin and add Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
  6. Only need the data? Mock it, and CORS never comes up.

CORS errors feel like the browser is in the way. It is doing its job: protecting your users from pages reading what they should not. While you develop, though, it is fine to tell your own browser to relax, on your own tab, for the requests you pick. That is one click with tweak.

items.title: Frontend Development Without a Backend: The Complete Guide
items.summary: Every frontend developer knows the feeling. The design is approved, the ticket is yours, and the API you need is "almost ready". Maybe the endpoint exists but returns an empty list. Maybe it exists only as a line in a spec document. Either way, you can't see your screen with real data, and you can't test what happens when that data is missing, slow or broken. This guide covers every practical way to build and test a frontend without a working backend: what each approach costs, where it shines, and how to pick one without turning your mocks into a second codebase. The problem: frontend work blocked by the backend ​ On most teams the frontend and the backend move at different speeds. A new feature usually needs both, and the frontend tends to be the one waiting. That wait shows up in a few familiar ways: The endpoint doesn't exist yet. You have a contract (an OpenAPI file, a Slack message, a whiteboard photo) but nothing answers the url. The endpoint exists, but the data is wrong for what you're building. Your staging account has three items and you need to see three hundred, or the field you render is always null . The states you need are hard to reach. An expired subscription, a 500 from the payments service, a response that takes eight seconds. They happen in production, rarely on purpose in development. The environment is unstable. Staging is down, a shared database was reset, or a dependency team is mid deploy. None of these are about writing frontend code. They're about not having the right responses at the right time. And that's the key insight behind every approach in this guide: your frontend doesn't need a backend, it needs responses. If you control what comes back from the network, you can build, test and demo the whole UI before a single endpoint is live. If you're new to the idea of mocking, why developers mock HTTP requests is a short primer on what a mock is and the trade offs it brings. The approaches, from simplest to most complete ​ There are four common ways to give a frontend responses it can't get from a backend yet. They aren't mutually exclusive, and many teams use more than one. 1. Hardcoded data in the component ​ The quickest thing that works: skip the request and put the data straight into the code. // TODO: replace with the real API call const orders = [ { id : 1 , status : 'shipped' , total : 42.5 } , { id : 2 , status : 'pending' , total : 18.0 } , ] Good for: the first hour of a prototype, when you only care about layout. The catch: your data fetching code never runs. Loading states, error handling, retries and caching are all untested, and the swap to the real API becomes a refactor instead of a config change. Hardcoded data also tends to outlive its TODO . 2. A local mock server ​ Run a small server on your machine that answers the endpoints you need: a JSON file served by a tool like json-server, an Express app with a few routes, or a mock server generated from an OpenAPI spec. Your app points its API base url at localhost during development. Good for: teams that want one shared fake backend, and APIs with a published contract you can generate from. The catch: it's another process to run and another project to maintain. Pointing the app at it means environment config, and possibly CORS headers on the mock server. And it only helps where your app talks to it: it does nothing for a deployed staging or production build. 3. In-app mocking libraries: MSW and Mirage JS ​ These libraries intercept requests inside your application, so your fetching code runs for real and the response comes from a handler you wrote. Mock Service Worker (MSW) registers a Service Worker in the browser that intercepts requests at the network level and answers them from request handlers you write in JavaScript. The same handlers can run in Node.js for tests. It's framework agnostic, widely adopted, and a strong choice when you want mocks that live in the repository and are shared with your test suite. Mirage JS runs an in-memory API server inside your app. It goes further than per-request responses: you can define models, factories and relationships, so a POST creates a record that a later GET returns. That makes it well suited to prototyping flows that depend on state. Good for: teams that want mocks version controlled next to the code, shared between development, Storybook and automated tests. The catch: they're code. You install a dependency, wire it into your app's startup, keep it out of production builds, and update the handlers whenever the API changes. That investment pays off for a long lived project with a test suite. It's a lot to set up just to see one screen with an error state. And because they're part of your build, they only exist where you shipped them, usually local development and tests. We compared one of these head to head in tweak vs Mock Service Worker , if you're choosing between them. 4. A browser extension ​ A browser extension can intercept the requests a page makes and answer them with the response you define, with no change to the app at all. tweak is one of these: you create a rule with a url, a method and the response you want, and every matching request gets that response. Good for: getting unblocked in minutes, testing states that are hard to reach, and working on any environment, including staging and production builds you can't modify. The catch: rules live in your browser, not your repository (you share them by exporting a file), and they don't run in your Node.js test suite. tweak intercepts the requests your page's JavaScript makes with fetch and XMLHttpRequest , which is where API calls come from. Every frontend developer knows the feeling. The design is approved, the ticket is yours, and the API you need is "almost ready". Maybe the endpoint exists but returns an empty list. Maybe it exists only as a line in a spec document. Either way, you can't see your screen with real data, and you can't test what happens when that data is missing, slow or broken. This guide covers every practical way to build and test a frontend without a working backend: what each approach costs, where it shines, and how to pick one without turning your mocks into a second codebase.

The problem: frontend work blocked by the backend​

On most teams the frontend and the backend move at different speeds. A new feature usually needs both, and the frontend tends to be the one waiting. That wait shows up in a few familiar ways:

  • The endpoint doesn't exist yet. You have a contract (an OpenAPI file, a Slack message, a whiteboard photo) but nothing answers the url.
  • The endpoint exists, but the data is wrong for what you're building. Your staging account has three items and you need to see three hundred, or the field you render is always null.
  • The states you need are hard to reach. An expired subscription, a 500 from the payments service, a response that takes eight seconds. They happen in production, rarely on purpose in development.
  • The environment is unstable. Staging is down, a shared database was reset, or a dependency team is mid deploy.

None of these are about writing frontend code. They're about not having the right responses at the right time. And that's the key insight behind every approach in this guide: your frontend doesn't need a backend, it needs responses. If you control what comes back from the network, you can build, test and demo the whole UI before a single endpoint is live.

If you're new to the idea of mocking, why developers mock HTTP requests is a short primer on what a mock is and the trade offs it brings.

The approaches, from simplest to most complete​

There are four common ways to give a frontend responses it can't get from a backend yet. They aren't mutually exclusive, and many teams use more than one.

1. Hardcoded data in the component​

The quickest thing that works: skip the request and put the data straight into the code.

// TODO: replace with the real API call
const orders = [
  { id: 1, status: 'shipped', total: 42.5 },
  { id: 2, status: 'pending', total: 18.0 },
]

Good for: the first hour of a prototype, when you only care about layout.

The catch: your data fetching code never runs. Loading states, error handling, retries and caching are all untested, and the swap to the real API becomes a refactor instead of a config change. Hardcoded data also tends to outlive its TODO.

2. A local mock server​

Run a small server on your machine that answers the endpoints you need: a JSON file served by a tool like json-server, an Express app with a few routes, or a mock server generated from an OpenAPI spec. Your app points its API base url at localhost during development.

Good for: teams that want one shared fake backend, and APIs with a published contract you can generate from.

The catch: it's another process to run and another project to maintain. Pointing the app at it means environment config, and possibly CORS headers on the mock server. And it only helps where your app talks to it: it does nothing for a deployed staging or production build.

3. In-app mocking libraries: MSW and Mirage JS​

These libraries intercept requests inside your application, so your fetching code runs for real and the response comes from a handler you wrote.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) registers a Service Worker in the browser that intercepts requests at the network level and answers them from request handlers you write in JavaScript. The same handlers can run in Node.js for tests. It's framework agnostic, widely adopted, and a strong choice when you want mocks that live in the repository and are shared with your test suite.

Mirage JS runs an in-memory API server inside your app. It goes further than per-request responses: you can define models, factories and relationships, so a POST creates a record that a later GET returns. That makes it well suited to prototyping flows that depend on state.

Good for: teams that want mocks version controlled next to the code, shared between development, Storybook and automated tests.

The catch: they're code. You install a dependency, wire it into your app's startup, keep it out of production builds, and update the handlers whenever the API changes. That investment pays off for a long lived project with a test suite. It's a lot to set up just to see one screen with an error state. And because they're part of your build, they only exist where you shipped them, usually local development and tests.

We compared one of these head to head in tweak vs Mock Service Worker, if you're choosing between them.

4. A browser extension​

A browser extension can intercept the requests a page makes and answer them with the response you define, with no change to the app at all. tweak is one of these: you create a rule with a url, a method and the response you want, and every matching request gets that response.

items.summary: Simple Modify Headers does what its name says: it adds, changes or removes HTTP headers on the requests your browser makes. If that is why you installed it, this post shows how tweak's headers only rule does the same job, for free, with a url per rule, real regex, one click templates, and a team that still ships updates. Where Simple Modify Headers is today ​ Simple Modify Headers still works, but it has gone quiet. Its last commit was in November 2024, and the newest release on its GitHub page is v1.8.1, from 2022. There are 30 open issues, some from 2022, with no visible answers. The move to Manifest V3 , the new platform browsers now require for extensions, also cost it features on Chrome. Its own README says so: Individual cookie modification is no longer possible, so the cookie options were removed. The "add" and "modify" actions now behave the same. Custom request filtering is no longer possible. And some limits were always there: One url pattern for the whole config. Every header rule shares the same url pattern, so "this header on site A, that header on site B" takes extra work. No regex. The pattern follows the browser's match pattern syntax, and you cannot set a port. Save to apply. Changes only apply once you click save. Open issues ask for things like filtering by HTTP method, folders for rules, and variables in header values. tweak already has all three. Simple Modify Headers vs tweak at a glance ​ Simple Modify Headers tweak Maintained Last commit November 2024 Yes, regular releases Manifest V3 Chrome only, Firefox on MV2 Yes, on every browser Browsers Chrome, Edge, Firefox Chrome, Edge, Firefox Request and response headers Yes Yes, free Set, Append, Remove Add and modify are the same Set, Append and Remove are different operations Url per rule No, one pattern for everything Yes Regex No Yes Filter by HTTP method No Yes Active tab only or always on No Active tab or Global Ready-made templates (CORS, cache) No Yes, free Bulk import headers from DevTools No Yes Notes on each rule A comment field Markdown label and notes Group rules in folders No Yes, collections (Tweak Basic) Variables in header values No Yes (Tweak Max) Mock API responses, redirects, more No Yes Account needed No No Price Free Header rules free, paid plans for advanced features How a header rule looks in tweak ​ Switch a rule to Headers only and you get a row per header, with a dropdown that picks the operation: There are two tabs, one per direction. Response headers change what comes back before the page sees it. Request headers change what goes out before it leaves the browser. Each rule has its own url expression and HTTP method. So one rule can set Authorization on your staging API, while another removes Content-Security-Policy on a different site, and neither gets in the other's way. Set, Append and Remove ​ Each row picks what to do with the header: Set replaces the value, or adds the header if it is missing. Append adds a value next to the existing one. Useful for a second Set-Cookie . Remove strips the header out. In Simple Modify Headers on Chrome, "add" and "modify" do the same thing. In tweak, Set and Append are two different operations, and both work. Browsers only allow Append on a fixed list of request headers. Pick it on any other one and tweak tells you right there, instead of silently doing nothing: Real regex, with a clear error ​ Simple Modify Headers matches with the browser's match patterns. tweak gives you the same simple url matching, plus a regex toggle when you need more. If the browser cannot compile your expression, the rule tells you, instead of looking enabled while doing nothing. Simple Modify Headers does what its name says: it adds, changes or removes HTTP headers on the requests your browser makes. If that is why you installed it, this post shows how tweak's headers only rule does the same job, for free, with a url per rule, real regex, one click templates, and a team that still ships updates.

Where Simple Modify Headers is today​

Simple Modify Headers still works, but it has gone quiet. Its last commit was in November 2024, and the newest release on its GitHub page is v1.8.1, from 2022. There are 30 open issues, some from 2022, with no visible answers.

The move to Manifest V3, the new platform browsers now require for extensions, also cost it features on Chrome. Its own README says so:

  • Individual cookie modification is no longer possible, so the cookie options were removed.
  • The "add" and "modify" actions now behave the same.
  • Custom request filtering is no longer possible.

And some limits were always there:

  • One url pattern for the whole config. Every header rule shares the same url pattern, so "this header on site A, that header on site B" takes extra work.
  • No regex. The pattern follows the browser's match pattern syntax, and you cannot set a port.
  • Save to apply. Changes only apply once you click save.

Open issues ask for things like filtering by HTTP method, folders for rules, and variables in header values. tweak already has all three.

Simple Modify Headers vs tweak at a glance​ Simple Modify HeaderstweakMaintainedLast commit November 2024Yes, regular releasesManifest V3Chrome only, Firefox on MV2Yes, on every browserBrowsersChrome, Edge, FirefoxChrome, Edge, FirefoxRequest and response headersYesYes, freeSet, Append, RemoveAdd and modify are the sameSet, Append and Remove are different operationsUrl per ruleNo, one pattern for everythingYesRegexNoYesFilter by HTTP methodNoYesActive tab only or always onNoActive tab or GlobalReady-made templates (CORS, cache)NoYes, freeBulk import headers from DevToolsNoYesNotes on each ruleA comment fieldMarkdown label and notesGroup rules in foldersNoYes, collections (Tweak Basic)Variables in header valuesNoYes (Tweak Max)Mock API responses, redirects, moreNoYesAccount neededNoNoPriceFreeHeader rules free, paid plans for advanced features How a header rule looks in tweak​

Switch a rule to Headers only and you get a row per header, with a dropdown that picks the operation:

There are two tabs, one per direction. Response headers change what comes back before the page sees it. Request headers change what goes out before it leaves the browser.

Each rule has its own url expression and HTTP method. So one rule can set Authorization on your staging API, while another removes Content-Security-Policy on a different site, and neither gets in the other's way.

Set, Append and Remove​

Each row picks what to do with the header:

  • Set replaces the value, or adds the header if it is missing.
  • Append adds a value next to the existing one. Useful for a second Set-Cookie.
  • Remove strips the header out.

In Simple Modify Headers on Chrome, "add" and "modify" do the same thing. In tweak, Set and Append are two different operations, and both work.

Browsers only allow Append on a fixed list of request headers. Pick it on any other one and tweak tells you right there, instead of silently doing nothing:

Real regex, with a clear error​

Simple Modify Headers matches with the browser's match patterns. tweak gives you the same simple url matching, plus a regex toggle when you need more. If the browser cannot compile your expression, the rule tells you, instead of looking enabled while doing nothing.

Active tab or always on​

Each rule has a Scope:

  • Active tab applies the rule only while tweak is running, on that tab. You never forget a header override on and wonder a week later why a site behaves oddly.
  • Global applies it on every tab, whether or not tweak is running, and survives a browser restart. Good for a header you simply want on all day.
No save button​

There is no save step. Edit a row and it applies.

Templates for the headers everyone sets​

Most people install a header extension for the same few jobs. tweak has them ready, one click away, all free:

TemplateWhat it doesCORS unblockSets the Access-Control-* response headers, so "blocked by CORS policy" goes awayDisable cacheSets Cache-Control: no-store and friends, so a reload always hits the serverCSP auditSets a strict Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, violations show in the consoleCSP offRemoves the page's Content-Security-Policy headers

Each one is a normal header rule once added, with notes that explain what it does. Edit it, narrow it to one site, or delete it. Read more in the templates docs.

Paste headers in bulk​

Copied a block of headers from DevTools, or have them as a JSON object? Paste them into a header rule and tweak turns them into rows, so you do not have to type them one by one:

Reaches every request​

A headers only rule is applied by the browser itself. It reaches every request the page makes, not only fetch and XHR calls: page navigations, scripts, images, stylesheets and fonts. It can also set headers a page's own JavaScript is not allowed to touch, like Referer, Origin and User-Agent.

More than headers​

Headers are often the first step. When you need more, the same extension has it:

  • Mock rules: return your own response, status code and body, with no server.
  • Modify rules: call the real server, then patch the response before the page reads it (Tweak Basic).
  • Redirect rules: send a request somewhere else, like your local server.
  • Block rules: cancel a request to see how the page handles a failure.
  • Collections: group rules in folders and switch between them (Tweak Basic).
  • Variables: put {{token}} in a header value and change it in one place (Tweak Max).
Moving over​
  1. Install tweak on Chrome, Edge or Firefox.
  2. Create a rule and switch it to Headers only.
  3. Use your Simple Modify Headers url pattern as the rule's url expression.
  4. Add a row per header: Set for "add" and "modify", Remove for "delete". Paste them in bulk if you have many.
  5. Pick Active tab while you test, and Global for headers you want always on.
  6. Turn Simple Modify Headers off, so two extensions are not changing the same headers.

No account and no sign-up. Header rules are free on every plan: request and response headers, every operation, both scopes.

The bottom line​

Simple Modify Headers is a fine, simple tool, and it served a lot of developers well. But it has gone quiet, Manifest V3 took features away on Chrome, and it still shares one url pattern across every rule.

tweak covers the same job for free, on Manifest V3, on Chrome, Edge and Firefox. You get a url and method per rule, regex, Set, Append and Remove as real operations, a clear scope, templates and bulk import. And when headers are not enough, mocks, redirects and the rest are right next to them.

Read the header rule docs or try tweak free.

items.title: How to Test Error States in Your Frontend Application
items.summary: The happy path gets tested every time someone opens the app. The error paths get tested when production breaks. That is backwards: an error screen is the one screen a user sees when they are already frustrated, and it is usually the least reviewed code in the project. The reason is simple: errors are hard to produce on demand . The backend works, so you cannot see what happens when it does not. This guide lists the failures worth testing, what a good UI does for each, and how to produce every one of them in the browser without changing a line of backend code. The failures worth testing ​ Not every status code deserves its own screen, but every kind of failure deserves a decision. These are the ones that show up in real apps: Failure What the user should see 500 , 502 , 503 A clear message, a retry action, and the rest of the page still working 404 on a detail page A "not found" state, not an infinite spinner or a blank card 401 mid-session A redirect to sign in, ideally back to where they were afterwards 403 "You do not have access", not a generic error 422 / 400 on a form The server's validation messages next to the right fields, input kept 429 A "slow down" message, and a retry that honours Retry-After Network error (offline, DNS) An offline message, and recovery when the connection comes back Timeout / very slow response A loading state that does not flicker, then a timeout with a retry Malformed JSON An error state, not an uncaught exception and a white screen Valid JSON, wrong shape Missing fields handled: no undefined on screen, no crash Empty list An empty state that tells the user what to do next Go through this table with your designer once. Every row you skip is a decision made by default, usually by a stack trace. Three ways to produce an error ​ 1. In code ​ Return the error from a mocked handler in your test suite ( Mock Service Worker , a stubbed fetch , a fixture server). This is the right place for the cases you want checked on every commit: one test per important row of the table above. The limit is that someone has to write and maintain each case, and nobody writes a handler to try something once. 2. In DevTools ​ The browser's developer tools can block a request ( Network request blocking ), slow the tab down ( throttling ), take it offline, and override a response's content locally ( Overrides ). They are already installed and they are good for a quick look. The limits: blocking only produces a network error, not a 500 ; overrides work on a saved copy of a response and take a few steps to set up; and the setup lives in one DevTools window. See our Network tab guide for where each of these lives. 3. In a browser extension ​ An extension like tweak sits between the page and the network, so you describe the failure as a rule and the page receives it as if the server had sent it. No code, no backend, works on localhost, staging and production alike. The rest of this guide uses it. Recipes ​ Each recipe is one rule. Create it in the tweak panel, refresh the page, look at the result, switch the rule off. A server error ( 500 , 503 ) ​ Create a Mock rule for the endpoint, set its status to 500 , and give it the body your API really returns on failure: { "error" : "internal_error" , "message" : "Something went wrong" } Now check: is there a message? A retry button? Does the retry call the endpoint again? Does the rest of the page still work, or did one failing widget take the whole route down? Our older post How to simulate an HTTP request error walks through this case with a demo app. An error on the real response ​ Sometimes you want the server's real answer with only the status changed, to see how the UI treats a 500 whose body is a normal payload. A Modify rule calls the real server and overrides the status, a field or a header (Modify rules are on Tweak Basic and Tweak Max). See How to override an HTTP status code . Session expired ( 401 ) ​ Mock the endpoint your app calls after a period of inactivity (often the user or token refresh endpoint) with status 401 . The right behaviour is a sign-in screen that brings the user back where they were. The common bug is a loop: the app retries, gets 401 , retries again. Validation errors ( 422 ) ​ Mock the form's submit endpoint with 422 and the error shape your backend uses: { "errors" : { "email" : [ "This email is already registered" ] , "password" : [ "Must be at least 12 characters" ] } } Check that each message lands next to its field, that what the user typed is still there, and that the submit button is usable again. Rate limited ( 429 ) ​ Mock the endpoint with status 429 , and add a Retry-After: 30 response header on the rule's Response headers tab. Does the app tell the user to wait, or does it retry in a tight loop and make things worse? Network failure ​ A network error is not a status code: the request never gets an answer, and fetch rejects instead of resolving. Your error handling for this lives in a different branch of the code (a catch , not an if (!response.ok) ), and it is often missing. Create a Block rule for the endpoint. The browser cancels the request and the page sees exactly what it would see on a dropped connection. To test the whole app offline, the toolbox's network tool takes the tab offline in one click. Slow responses and timeouts ​ Set a delay on a Mock rule (for example 8000 ms) to see the loading state for as long as you want. Check that the skeleton does not jump when the data arrives, that the user can still navigate away, and, if your client has a timeout, that the timeout message shows up. See How to simulate a delayed HTTP request . To slow the whole tab down to a real connection (Slow 3G, hotel wifi), use the toolbox's network tool instead. Malformed JSON ​ Mock the endpoint with status 200 and a body that is not valid JSON: {"items": [{"id": 1, "name": "Mug" tweak will warn you on the rule that the payload is invalid, and serve it anyway, because here that is the point. A good app shows an error state. A fragile one throws inside response.json() and leaves a white screen. Valid JSON, wrong shape ​ This is the error that ships to production most often, because the API "worked". Mock the response with a field missing or null : { "id" : 42 , "name" : null , "price" : { "amount" : 1999 } } Here the currency is gone and the name is null . Look for undefined , NaN , null and empty strings on screen, and for crashes deeper in the tree. With a Modify rule you can do this on the real response, removing one field and keeping the rest. Empty states ​ Mock the list endpoint with [] (or { "items": [], "total": 0 } ). An empty state is not an error, but it is a state nobody sees in development because the dev database is never empty. Make it a routine ​ Keep a collection of failure rules per feature: "Checkout: 500", "Checkout: offline", "Checkout: slow". Collections (Tweak Basic and Tweak Max) group them; on the free plan, a clear label on each rule does the job. Share them. Export the rules to a JSON file and commit it, so QA and the next developer get the same failures. Test the error states in review. A pull request that adds a screen should say what the screen does on a 500 , on a network error and on an empty response. With the rules ready, that takes a minute to check. Promote the important ones to automated tests. When a failure case matters every release, write it as a handler in your test suite too. The happy path gets tested every time someone opens the app. The error paths get tested when production breaks. That is backwards: an error screen is the one screen a user sees when they are already frustrated, and it is usually the least reviewed code in the project. The reason is simple: errors are hard to produce on demand. The backend works, so you cannot see what happens when it does not.

This guide lists the failures worth testing, what a good UI does for each, and how to produce every one of them in the browser without changing a line of backend code.

The failures worth testing​

Not every status code deserves its own screen, but every kind of failure deserves a decision. These are the ones that show up in real apps:

FailureWhat the user should see500, 502, 503A clear message, a retry action, and the rest of the page still working404 on a detail pageA "not found" state, not an infinite spinner or a blank card401 mid-sessionA redirect to sign in, ideally back to where they were afterwards403"You do not have access", not a generic error422 / 400 on a formThe server's validation messages next to the right fields, input kept429A "slow down" message, and a retry that honours Retry-AfterNetwork error (offline, DNS)An offline message, and recovery when the connection comes backTimeout / very slow responseA loading state that does not flicker, then a timeout with a retryMalformed JSONAn error state, not an uncaught exception and a white screenValid JSON, wrong shapeMissing fields handled: no undefined on screen, no crashEmpty listAn empty state that tells the user what to do next

Go through this table with your designer once. Every row you skip is a decision made by default, usually by a stack trace.

Three ways to produce an error​ 1. In code​

Return the error from a mocked handler in your test suite (Mock Service Worker, a stubbed fetch, a fixture server). This is the right place for the cases you want checked on every commit: one test per important row of the table above.

The limit is that someone has to write and maintain each case, and nobody writes a handler to try something once.

2. In DevTools​

The browser's developer tools can block a request (Network request blocking), slow the tab down (throttling), take it offline, and override a response's content locally (Overrides). They are already installed and they are good for a quick look. The limits: blocking only produces a network error, not a 500; overrides work on a saved copy of a response and take a few steps to set up; and the setup lives in one DevTools window. See our Network tab guide for where each of these lives.

3. In a browser extension​

An extension like tweak sits between the page and the network, so you describe the failure as a rule and the page receives it as if the server had sent it. No code, no backend, works on localhost, staging and production alike. The rest of this guide uses it.

Recipes​

Each recipe is one rule. Create it in the tweak panel, refresh the page, look at the result, switch the rule off.

A server error (500, 503)​

Create a Mock rule for the endpoint, set its status to 500, and give it the body your API really returns on failure:

{ "error": "internal_error", "message": "Something went wrong" }

Now check: is there a message? A retry button? Does the retry call the endpoint again? Does the rest of the page still work, or did one failing widget take the whole route down?

Our older post How to simulate an HTTP request error walks through this case with a demo app.

An error on the real response​

Sometimes you want the server's real answer with only the status changed, to see how the UI treats a 500 whose body is a normal payload. A Modify rule calls the real server and overrides the status, a field or a header (Modify rules are on Tweak Basic and Tweak Max). See How to override an HTTP status code.

Session expired (401)​

Mock the endpoint your app calls after a period of inactivity (often the user or token refresh endpoint) with status 401. The right behaviour is a sign-in screen that brings the user back where they were. The common bug is a loop: the app retries, gets 401, retries again.

Validation errors (422)​

Mock the form's submit endpoint with 422 and the error shape your backend uses:

{
  "errors": {
    "email": ["This email is already registered"],
    "password": ["Must be at least 12 characters"]
  }
}

Check that each message lands next to its field, that what the user typed is still there, and that the submit button is usable again.

Rate limited (429)​

Mock the endpoint with status 429, and add a Retry-After: 30 response header on the rule's Response headers tab. Does the app tell the user to wait, or does it retry in a tight loop and make things worse?

Network failure​

A network error is not a status code: the request never gets an answer, and fetch rejects instead of resolving. Your error handling for this lives in a different branch of the code (a catch, not an if (!response.ok)), and it is often missing.

Create a Block rule for the endpoint. The browser cancels the request and the page sees exactly what it would see on a dropped connection. To test the whole app offline, the toolbox's network tool takes the tab offline in one click.

Slow responses and timeouts​

Set a delay on a Mock rule (for example 8000 ms) to see the loading state for as long as you want. Check that the skeleton does not jump when the data arrives, that the user can still navigate away, and, if your client has a timeout, that the timeout message shows up. See How to simulate a delayed HTTP request.

To slow the whole tab down to a real connection (Slow 3G, hotel wifi), use the toolbox's network tool instead.

Malformed JSON​

Mock the endpoint with status 200 and a body that is not valid JSON:

{"items": [{"id": 1, "name": "Mug"

tweak will warn you on the rule that the payload is invalid, and serve it anyway, because here that is the point. A good app shows an error state. A fragile one throws inside response.json() and leaves a white screen.

Valid JSON, wrong shape​

This is the error that ships to production most often, because the API "worked". Mock the response with a field missing or null:

{ "id": 42, "name": null, "price": { "amount": 1999 } }

Here the currency is gone and the name is null. Look for undefined, NaN, null and empty strings on screen, and for crashes deeper in the tree. With a Modify rule you can do this on the real response, removing one field and keeping the rest.

Empty states​

Mock the list endpoint with [] (or { "items": [], "total": 0 }). An empty state is not an error, but it is a state nobody sees in development because the dev database is never empty.

Make it a routine​
  • Keep a collection of failure rules per feature: "Checkout: 500", "Checkout: offline", "Checkout: slow". Collections (Tweak Basic and Tweak Max) group them; on the free plan, a clear label on each rule does the job.
  • Share them. Export the rules to a JSON file and commit it, so QA and the next developer get the same failures.
  • Test the error states in review. A pull request that adds a screen should say what the screen does on a 500, on a network error and on an empty response. With the rules ready, that takes a minute to check.
  • Promote the important ones to automated tests. When a failure case matters every release, write it as a handler in your test suite too.
Summary​

Every failure in the table above can be produced in the browser, on demand, without the backend's help: a status code and a body for server errors, a blocked request for network errors, a delay for slow responses, a broken or reshaped body for parsing errors. The only thing standing between your app and good error handling is how easy it is to see the errors, and that part is solved.

Install tweak and create your first error rule. Mock and Block rules are free.
